questions.question: Which one of the following materials cannot be used to make a lens?
options: Water
Glass
Plastic
Clay
questions.explanation: Clay is opaque and cannot form a transparent lens.

questions.question: The image formed by a concave mirror is observed to be virtual, erect and larger than the object. Where should be the position of the object?
options: Between the principal focus and the centre of curvature
At the centre of curvature
Beyond the centre of curvature
Between the pole of the mirror and its principal focus
questions.explanation: Virtual, erect, enlarged images from a concave mirror occur when the object is between P and F.

questions.question: In the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, which sign convention is used for distances measured against the direction of incident light?
options: They are taken as positive
They are taken as negative
Sign does not matter
Only u is negative
questions.explanation: Distances measured against the direction of incident light are negative in the NCERT sign convention.

questions.question: Refractive index n = c/v compares the speed of light in vacuum to that in the medium. If light slows down in glass, n is
options: less than 1
equal to 1
greater than 1
zero
questions.explanation: When v < c, the ratio c/v exceeds 1.

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Non-luminous objects**?
options: See the path: source → object → eye.
Darkness means insufficient light reaching the eye.
Non-luminous ≠ invisible
Reflection sends light back; it does not create new light.
questions.explanation: Non-luminous ≠ invisible. Reflection makes them visible.
questions.category_label: Day 1 — How We See and Represent Light · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Light source**?
options: A beam = many rays; a ray diagram often shows one representative ray.
Always ask: where did the light start?.
Light rays are drawn straight until reflection or refraction changes direction.
Draw the full path before deciding where an image forms.
questions.explanation: Always ask: where did the light start?
questions.category_label: Day 1 — How We See and Represent Light · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Which statement best describes **Luminous objects**?
options: A beam is a collection of many rays travelling together, often from a torch or sunlight through clouds.
Vision happens when light from an object enters your eye and forms a signal for your brain.
A ray is a straight line with an arrow showing the direction light travels.
A luminous object produces its own light.
questions.explanation: Luminous means the object is the light source — not just bright-looking.
questions.category_label: Day 1 — How We See and Represent Light · Recall — definitions and key facts

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Incident ray**?
options: Mark this point before drawing the normal.
Measure reflection angles from the normal, not from the mirror.
Same plane means one 2D diagram is enough for plane mirrors.
Incident = incoming; arrow points to the surface
questions.explanation: Incident = incoming; arrow points to the surface.
questions.category_label: Day 2 — Reflection and Plane Mirrors · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Reflected ray**?
options: Reflected ray arrow points away from the mirror
Shiny and smooth surfaces give clearer reflections.
Same side rule: both angles are measured from the normal on opposite sides of it.
i = r (both measured from the normal).
questions.explanation: Reflected ray arrow points away from the mirror.
questions.category_label: Day 2 — Reflection and Plane Mirrors · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Which statement best describes **Reflecting surface**?
options: The normal is an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.
The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
A reflecting surface sends light back instead of absorbing it.
A plane mirror gives a virtual, erect image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
questions.explanation: Shiny and smooth surfaces give clearer reflections.
questions.category_label: Day 2 — Reflection and Plane Mirrors · Recall — definitions and key facts

questions.question: A spherical mirror and a thin spherical lens have each a focal length of –15 cm. The mirror and the lens are likely to be
options: both concave
both convex
the mirror is concave and the lens is convex
the mirror is convex, but the lens is concave
questions.explanation: Negative focal length (New Cartesian sign convention) indicates a concave mirror and a concave (diverging) lens.

questions.question: No matter how far you stand from a mirror, your image appears erect. The mirror is likely to be
options: only plane
only concave
only convex
either plane or convex
questions.explanation: Plane and convex mirrors always give erect images; concave mirrors can give inverted real images.

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Light entering the eye**?
options: Non-luminous ≠ invisible.
Luminous means the object is the light source — not just bright-looking.
Reflection sends light back; it does not create new light.
See the path: source → object → eye
questions.explanation: See the path: source → object → eye.
questions.category_label: Day 1 — How We See and Represent Light · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Seeing in darkness**?
options: Light rays are drawn straight until reflection or refraction changes direction.
Draw the full path before deciding where an image forms.
Darkness means insufficient light reaching the eye
Always ask: where did the light start?.
questions.explanation: Darkness means insufficient light reaching the eye.
questions.category_label: Day 1 — How We See and Represent Light · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Which statement best describes **Reflected light**?
options: To explain seeing: light leaves a source, hits an object (often by reflection), then enters your eye.
A beam is a collection of many rays travelling together, often from a torch or sunlight through clouds.
Vision happens when light from an object enters your eye and forms a signal for your brain.
When light hits a surface and bounces back, that bounced light is reflected light.
questions.explanation: Reflection sends light back; it does not create new light.
questions.category_label: Day 1 — How We See and Represent Light · Recall — definitions and key facts

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **The normal**?
options: Mark this point before drawing the normal.
Use the arc between incident ray and normal — not the surface.
Measure reflection angles from the normal, not from the mirror
Reflected ray arrow points away from the mirror.
questions.explanation: Measure reflection angles from the normal, not from the mirror.
questions.category_label: Day 2 — Reflection and Plane Mirrors · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Angle of incidence**?
options: Reflected ray arrow points away from the mirror.
Same side rule: both angles are measured from the normal on opposite sides of it.
Use the arc between incident ray and normal — not the surface
Shiny and smooth surfaces give clearer reflections.
questions.explanation: Use the arc between incident ray and normal — not the surface.
questions.category_label: Day 2 — Reflection and Plane Mirrors · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Which statement best describes **Point of incidence**?
options: The angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the normal at the point of incidence.
The point of incidence is the exact spot on the surface where the incident ray meets it.
The normal is an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.
The reflected ray leaves the surface after reflection.
questions.explanation: Mark this point before drawing the normal.
questions.category_label: Day 2 — Reflection and Plane Mirrors · Recall — definitions and key facts

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Concave mirror**?
options: Convex = bulges out toward the object.
Draw rays hitting the polished arc, not the back.
C is outside the mirror surface.
Concave = cave-like = curves in
questions.explanation: Concave = cave-like = curves in.
questions.category_label: Day 3 — Spherical Mirrors · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Convex mirror**?
options: Convex = bulges out toward the object
R = 2f for small-aperture spherical mirrors.
P is on the mirror; C is not on the mirror.
Large mirrors break the small-angle approximation used in school formulas.
questions.explanation: Convex = bulges out toward the object.
questions.category_label: Day 3 — Spherical Mirrors · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens to get a real image of the size of the object?
options: At the principal focus of the lens
At twice the focal length
At infinity
Between the optical centre of the lens and its principal focus
questions.explanation: At u = 2f, a convex lens forms a real image of the same size at v = 2f.

questions.question: Which of the following lenses would you prefer to use while reading small letters found in a dictionary?
options: A convex lens of focal length 50 cm
A concave lens of focal length 50 cm
A convex lens of focal length 5 cm
A concave lens of focal length 5 cm
questions.explanation: A convex lens is a magnifier; shorter focal length gives greater magnification for nearby objects.

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Direction of incident light**?
options: Down from axis = −.
Light goes left → right
Up from axis = +.
Real object in front → u positive.
questions.explanation: Light goes left → right.
questions.category_label: Day 9 — Mirror Sign Convention · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Positive horizontal**?
options: Down from axis = −.
Real v +, virtual v −.
Concave: f negative.
With the light: positive
questions.explanation: With the light: positive.
questions.category_label: Day 9 — Mirror Sign Convention · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Which statement best describes **Pole as origin**?
options: Distances measured against incident light (behind the mirror) are negative.
In the mirror formula sign convention, pole P is taken as the origin (0) for distances.
For a real object in front of the mirror, u is taken positive in the NCERT convention.
Incident light is treated as travelling from left to right in standard NCERT diagrams.
questions.explanation: P = 0 on the axis.
questions.category_label: Day 9 — Mirror Sign Convention · Recall — definitions and key facts

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Image distance v**?
options: Signs first, numbers second.
Always include sign of f in 1/f.
Negative m → inverted image.
v sign tells real vs virtual
questions.explanation: v sign tells real vs virtual.
questions.category_label: Day 10 — Mirror Formula and Magnification · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Focal length f**?
options: Add reciprocals, not distances directly.
Reciprocal form — not v = f + u.
Always include sign of f in 1/f
Measure u from P to object.
questions.explanation: Always include sign of f in 1/f.
questions.category_label: Day 10 — Mirror Formula and Magnification · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Which statement best describes **Object distance u**?
options: Substitute signed u, v, f before solving — signs are part of the physics.
u is the distance of the object from pole P along the principal axis.
After calculating m, state: inverted/erect, enlarged/diminished/same, using sign and |m|.
1/v + 1/u = 1/f relates object distance, image distance, and focal length.
questions.explanation: Measure u from P to object.
questions.category_label: Day 10 — Mirror Formula and Magnification · Recall — definitions and key facts

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Boundary between media**?
options: Speed change → bending.
Denser = slower light.
Transparent ≠ no refraction.
Boundary = interface between media
questions.explanation: Boundary = interface between media.
questions.category_label: Day 11 — Introduction to Refraction · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Incident ray at boundary**?
options: Speed change → bending.
Incident ray in first medium
Transparent ≠ no refraction.
Rarer = faster light.
questions.explanation: Incident ray in first medium.
questions.category_label: Day 11 — Introduction to Refraction · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Ray of light**?
options: A beam = many rays; a ray diagram often shows one representative ray.
One arrow = one direction of light travel
Light rays are drawn straight until reflection or refraction changes direction.
Draw the full path before deciding where an image forms.
questions.explanation: One arrow = one direction of light travel.
questions.category_label: Day 1 — How We See and Represent Light · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Beam of light**?
options: Light rays are drawn straight until reflection or refraction changes direction.
A beam = many rays; a ray diagram often shows one representative ray
Always ask: where did the light start?.
Luminous means the object is the light source — not just bright-looking.
questions.explanation: A beam = many rays; a ray diagram often shows one representative ray.
questions.category_label: Day 1 — How We See and Represent Light · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Which statement best describes **Straight-line propagation**?
options: In a uniform medium, light travels in straight lines.
Vision happens when light from an object enters your eye and forms a signal for your brain.
A ray is a straight line with an arrow showing the direction light travels.
A beam is a collection of many rays travelling together, often from a torch or sunlight through clouds.
questions.explanation: Light rays are drawn straight until reflection or refraction changes direction.
questions.category_label: Day 1 — How We See and Represent Light · Recall — definitions and key facts

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **First law of reflection**?
options: i = r (both measured from the normal)
Measure reflection angles from the normal, not from the mirror.
Shiny and smooth surfaces give clearer reflections.
Reflected ray arrow points away from the mirror.
questions.explanation: i = r (both measured from the normal).
questions.category_label: Day 2 — Reflection and Plane Mirrors · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Second law of reflection**?
options: i = r (both measured from the normal).
Same side rule: both angles are measured from the normal on opposite sides of it.
Reflected ray arrow points away from the mirror.
Same plane means one 2D diagram is enough for plane mirrors
questions.explanation: Same plane means one 2D diagram is enough for plane mirrors.
questions.category_label: Day 2 — Reflection and Plane Mirrors · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Which statement best describes **Angle of reflection**?
options: A reflecting surface sends light back instead of absorbing it.
A plane mirror gives a virtual, erect image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
The angle of reflection is measured between the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence.
questions.explanation: Same side rule: both angles are measured from the normal on opposite sides of it.
questions.category_label: Day 2 — Reflection and Plane Mirrors · Recall — definitions and key facts

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Pole (P)**?
options: Draw rays hitting the polished arc, not the back.
P is on the mirror; C is not on the mirror
Spherical = part of a sphere; not flat like a plane mirror.
Principal axis passes through P and C.
questions.explanation: P is on the mirror; C is not on the mirror.
questions.category_label: Day 3 — Spherical Mirrors · Apply — examples and reasoning

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Centre of curvature (C)**?
options: Ask: does the mirror surface hug the centre or push away from it?.
R = 2f for small-aperture spherical mirrors.
C is outside the mirror surface
Draw rays hitting the polished arc, not the back.
questions.explanation: C is outside the mirror surface.
questions.category_label: Day 3 — Spherical Mirrors · Avoid mistakes — common confusions

questions.question: Which statement best describes **Spherical reflecting surface**?
options: A spherical mirror is part of a sphere's surface.
The pole P is the centre point of the mirror's reflecting surface.
C is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror forms a part.
A concave mirror curves inward (reflecting surface faces the centre of the sphere).
questions.explanation: Spherical = part of a sphere; not flat like a plane mirror.
questions.category_label: Day 3 — Spherical Mirrors · Recall — definitions and key facts

questions.question: What is the key takeaway about **Focal length (f)**?
options: f is measured from P to F — not from C to F unless you know R = 2f
Real focus = rays actually cross.
Concave = converging.
R = 2f → F lies midway between P and C.
questions.explanation: f is measured from P to F — not from C to F unless you know R = 2f.
questions.category_label: Day 4 — Focus and Mirror Ray Behaviour · Apply — examples and reasoning
